title: No. 54 — The Apportionment of Members Among the States (Madison)
paragraphs: The next matter I will examine concerning the House of Representatives is the apportionment of its members among the several States. This is to be determined by the same rule used for direct taxes.

It is not disputed that the number of people in each State should be the standard for regulating the proportion of representatives for each State. The establishment of the same rule for apportioning taxes will probably be little contested either, though the rule itself in this case is by no means founded on the same principle. In the former case, the rule refers to the personal rights of the people, with which it has a natural and universal connection. In the latter, it refers to the proportion of wealth, of which it is in no case a precise measure, and in ordinary cases a very poor one. But despite the imperfection of the rule when applied to the relative wealth and contributions of the States, it is clearly the least objectionable among the practicable rules. It had too recently received the general sanction of America not to find a ready preference with the convention.

All this will perhaps be admitted, it may be said. But does it follow, from admitting numbers as the measure of representation, or slaves combined with free citizens as a ratio of taxation, that slaves ought to be included in the numerical rule of representation? Slaves are considered as property, not as persons. They ought therefore to be included in estimates of taxation, which are based on property, and excluded from representation, which is regulated by a census of persons. This is the objection, as I understand it, stated in its full force. I shall be equally candid in stating the reasoning that may be offered on the opposite side.

"We subscribe to the doctrine," one of our Southern brethren might observe, "that representation relates more immediately to persons, and taxation more immediately to property. We agree in applying this distinction to the case of our slaves. But we must deny the claim that slaves are considered merely as property, and in no respect as persons. The true state of the case is that they share both qualities. Our laws consider them, in some respects, as persons, and in other respects as property. In being compelled to labor, not for himself but for a master; in being able to be sold by one master to another; and in being subject at all times to be restrained in his liberty and chastised in his body by the capricious will of another — the slave may appear to be degraded from the human rank and classed with those irrational animals which the law calls property. But on the other hand, in being protected in his life and limbs against the violence of all others, even the master of his labor and his liberty; and in being himself punishable for all violence committed against others — the slave is no less clearly regarded by the law as a member of society, not as a part of irrational creation; as a moral person, not as a mere article of property. The federal Constitution therefore decides with great propriety on the case of our slaves when it views them in the mixed character of persons and property. This is in fact their true character. It is the character bestowed on them by the laws under which they live. It will not be denied that these laws are the proper criterion. For it is only on the pretext that the laws have transformed the negroes into property that their place in the count of numbers is disputed. And it is admitted that if the laws were to restore the rights that have been taken away, the negroes could no longer be refused an equal share of representation with the other inhabitants.

"This question may be placed in another light. It is agreed on all sides that numbers are the best scale of wealth and taxation, just as they are the only proper scale of representation. Would the convention have been impartial or consistent if they had rejected the slaves from the list of inhabitants when shares of representation were calculated, but inserted them on the list when the tariff of contributions was adjusted? Could it reasonably be expected that the Southern States would join in a system that considered their slaves in some degree as men when burdens were to be imposed, but refused to consider them in the same light when advantages were to be conferred? Might not some surprise also be expressed that those who reproach the Southern States with the barbarous policy of considering as property a part of their human brethren should themselves contend that the government to which all the States are parties ought to consider this unfortunate race more completely in the unnatural light of property than the very laws of which they complain?

"It may be replied, perhaps, that slaves are not included in the count of representatives in any of the States that hold them. They neither vote themselves nor add to the votes of their masters. On what principle, then, ought they to be taken into the federal estimate of representation? In rejecting them altogether, the Constitution would, in this respect, have followed the very laws that have been appealed to as the proper guide.

"This objection is repelled by a single observation. It is a fundamental principle of the proposed Constitution that, just as the total number of representatives allotted to the several States is determined by a federal rule based on the total number of inhabitants, so the right of choosing this allotted number in each State is to be exercised by such part of the inhabitants as the State itself may designate. The qualifications on which the right of suffrage depends are perhaps not the same in any two States. In some States the difference is very material. In every State, a certain proportion of inhabitants are deprived of this right by the State constitution, who will nevertheless be included in the census by which the federal Constitution apportions the representatives. From this point of view, the Southern States might retort the complaint by insisting that the principle laid down by the convention required no regard be had to the policy of particular States toward their own inhabitants. Consequently, the slaves, as inhabitants, should have been admitted to the census according to their full number, just like other inhabitants who, by the policy of other States, are not admitted to all the rights of citizens. A rigorous adherence to this principle, however, is waived by those who would gain by it. All they ask is that equal moderation be shown on the other side. Let the case of the slaves be considered as it is in truth, a peculiar one. Let the compromise expedient of the Constitution be mutually adopted, which regards them as inhabitants but as debased by servitude below the equal level of free inhabitants — which regards the SLAVE as divested of two-fifths of the MAN.

"After all, may not another ground be taken on which this article of the Constitution will admit a still readier defense? We have so far proceeded on the idea that representation related to persons only, and not at all to property. But is it a just idea? Government is instituted no less for protection of property than of persons. The one as well as the other, therefore, may be considered as represented by those charged with the government. On this principle, in several of the States, and particularly in the State of New York, one branch of the government is intended more especially to be the guardian of property. It is accordingly elected by that part of society most interested in this object of government. In the federal Constitution, this policy does not prevail. The rights of property are committed to the same hands as the personal rights. Some attention ought, therefore, to be paid to property in the choice of those hands.

"For another reason, the votes allowed in the federal legislature to the people of each State ought to bear some proportion to the comparative wealth of the States. States have not, like individuals, an influence over each other arising from superior advantages of fortune. If the law allows a wealthy citizen but a single vote in choosing his representative, the respect and consequence he derives from his fortunate situation very frequently guide the votes of others to the candidates of his choice. Through this imperceptible channel the rights of property are conveyed into public representation. A State possesses no such influence over other States. It is not probable that the richest State in the Confederacy will ever influence the choice of a single representative in any other State. Nor will the representatives of the larger and richer States possess any other advantage in the federal legislature, over the representatives of other States, than what may result from their superior number alone. As far, therefore, as their superior wealth and weight may justly entitle them to any advantage, it ought to be secured to them by a superior share of representation. The new Constitution is, in this respect, materially different from the existing Confederation, as well as from that of the United Netherlands and other similar confederacies. In each of the latter, the effect of the federal resolutions depends on the subsequent and voluntary resolutions of the states composing the union. Hence the states, though possessing an equal vote in the public councils, have unequal influence corresponding with the unequal importance of these subsequent and voluntary resolutions. Under the proposed Constitution, the federal acts will take effect without the necessary intervention of the individual States. They will depend merely on the majority of votes in the federal legislature. Consequently each vote, whether from a larger or smaller State, or a State more or less wealthy or powerful, will have an equal weight and effect — in the same manner as votes individually given in a State legislature, by the representatives of unequal counties or other districts, have each a precise equality of value and effect. If there is any difference in the case, it proceeds from the difference in the personal character of the individual representative, rather than from any regard to the extent of the district from which he comes."

Such is the reasoning that an advocate for the Southern interests might use on this subject. Although it may seem a little strained at some points, on the whole I must confess that it fully reconciles me to the scale of representation which the convention has established.

In one respect, establishing a common measure for representation and taxation will have a very salutary effect. The accuracy of the census obtained by Congress will necessarily depend, to a considerable degree, on the willingness, if not the cooperation, of the States. It is therefore very important that the States feel as little bias as possible to either inflate or reduce the count of their numbers. Were their share of representation alone governed by this rule, they would have an interest in exaggerating their inhabitants. Were the rule to decide their share of taxation alone, the contrary temptation would prevail. By extending the rule to both objects, the States will have opposite interests, which will check and balance each other and produce the necessary impartiality.
